ORM, DbContext, tracking and desktop EF CRUD

Use an EF Core context from the desktop app to save and load student objects.

Open interactive lesson and complete code

What you are building

A desktop student register

Build a WPF window to add, show, edit and remove students. Compare database storage with exporting data as a JSON text file.

The example can use SQLite or SQL Server. JSON export creates a separate file.

Check the result

Run the Windows desktop app, add a student, select the row and try editing it.

An ORM maps objects to rows. In the desktop lab, choose EF Core SQLite to use a local file database instead of manually writing SQL.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

The building blocks

  • Entity: Student, a C# object that represents data. DbSet: Students, the queryable collection for that entity.
  • DbContext: the short-lived unit of work that holds configuration and change tracking. Database provider: Sqlite translates supported EF operations to SQLite commands.
  • The in-memory model is EF’s description of entity types, keys, properties and relationships. It is not the same thing as the EF InMemory test provider.
  • Migrations describe schema changes. Change tracking describes entity changes. SaveChanges sends database modifications. Navigation properties describe relationships between entities.

Follow desktop CRUD

The sample creates a fresh SchoolDb for each operation. This avoids leaving a long-lived UI context with stale tracked objects. Add and SaveChanges create rows; Update attaches an edited row; Remove deletes it. AsNoTracking is used for read-only lists. EnsureCreated is used only for this self-contained desktop teaching database; it is not a schema-evolution plan. Use migrations for an evolving real application.

Expected persistence

Create a row, close the window and reopen it, then choose Read. The row remains in the LocalApplicationData database. Deleting the application process does not delete the file. Do not share one DbContext across simultaneous background threads.

Try it yourself

Explain model versus database schema.

Worked answer

The model is the application’s mapping description. The schema is the actual database structure; migrations help keep them aligned.

Why is a new context per desktop operation helpful?

Worked answer

It limits tracking lifetime, resource ownership and stale state. A more advanced UI can use IDbContextFactory to create contexts for operations.

Predict and practise

Does changing an object always immediately save the database?

Check your prediction

No. The context needs SaveChanges or SaveChangesAsync for tracked changes to be stored.
